# Anthropic Python SDK v1.13.0 adds Managed Agents workflows, multiagent config and thread status filtering

Anthropic released v1.13.0 of its Python SDK, adding workflows, multiagent configuration and thread status filtering to Managed Agents. The release also adds types for the Chat and Cowork unified analytics metrics API. No new model is included.

October 9, 2026 · 3:35 PM 2 min read

Anthropic's Python SDK v1.13.0 adds workflows, multiagent configuration and thread status filtering to the Managed Agents API surface. The release also adds types for the Chat and Cowork unified analytics metrics API. It is an SDK update only and does not introduce a new model.

## What changed in v1.13.0

The release was published by the `anthropic-sdks-releaser` account on the `anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python` GitHub repository, tagged at commit `b4b7916`. The release notes list two features and one chore.

Features

- Analytics types: The SDK adds types for the Chat and Cowork unified analytics metrics API.
- Managed Agents: The SDK adds workflows, multiagent configuration and thread status filtering to Managed Agents.

Chores

- Internal: The default API version header value is now named in the code. This is a refactor and is not described as a behavior change.

The release carries two assets.

## What the release notes do not say

The notes are terse, and several details are not disclosed:

- Field-level schemas for the new workflow and multiagent configuration parameters are not described in the notes.
- The notes do not say which thread statuses can be filtered.
- It is not stated whether the new Managed Agents features are generally available or in beta. Developers should check the API documentation and the SDK's type definitions before relying on them.
- No breaking changes are listed.
- No model versions, context window changes, pricing changes or benchmark results are part of this release. Pricing is not applicable.

The notes show a release timestamp of 09 Oct, 15:28, without a year or time zone.

## What this means

The notable change is the expansion of Managed Agents. Workflows and multiagent configuration point to Anthropic extending that surface from single-agent use toward orchestrating several agents within one managed setup. That reading is inferred from the feature names alone, as the release notes give no design details. Thread status filtering is a practical addition for anyone running many agent threads, since it lets clients query by state rather than fetching and filtering locally.

The analytics types matter for a narrower group: teams that consume usage metrics across Chat and Cowork. Typed responses reduce the need for hand-written models and make the data easier to integrate into internal dashboards.

For developers, this is a minor-version feature release. Teams already using Managed Agents should review the SDK diff and the API reference to confirm the exact parameters. Everyone else can treat it as a routine upgrade. Because the notes list no breaking changes, upgrades should be low risk, but pinning versions and running existing tests first remains standard practice.

Anthropic's Python SDK v1.13.0 Quietly Ships Multi-Agent Plumbing — Tessera

# Anthropic's Python SDK v1.13.0 Quietly Ships Multi-Agent Plumbing

Anthropic's anthropic-sdk-python v1.13.0 adds multiagent configuration and thread status filtering to Managed Agents, plus analytics types. The quiet release says a lot about…

 Tessera Newsroom · 5 min read · October 10, 2026 

The gist

- Anthropic's v1.13.0 SDK adds multiagent configuration, workflows, and thread status filtering to Managed Agents, signaling operational maturity.
- Unified Chat and Cowork analytics types suggest a consolidation play across Anthropic's consumer and team product surfaces.
- Anthropic aims to own the orchestration layer, keeping developers inside its API rather than third-party frameworks like LangGraph.

Anthropic shipped anthropic-sdk-python v1.13.0 on October 9, and the release notes are three lines long. That is the whole story on its face: two feature bullets and a chore. But read the bullets carefully and you get a decent map of where Anthropic thinks its agent products are going, because SDK changelogs are the least glamorous and most honest signal a lab emits. Marketing pages tell you what a company wants you to believe. Type definitions tell you what its API actually accepts.

The two features are worth separating. The first adds types for “Chat and Cowork unified analytics metrics.” The second adds “workflows, multiagent configuration and thread status filtering to Managed Agents.” The chore renames the default API version header value internally, which is the kind of thing that matters only to people who have been burned by a silent header change in a pinned dependency.

## What “Managed Agents” now accepts

The phrase to sit with is “multiagent configuration.” Anthropic has been selling agents as a product surface for a while, and the SDK already exposed the primitives you would expect: tool use, message threads, streaming. What v1.13.0 adds is the configuration layer for running more than one agent against a shared problem, plus the ability to filter threads by status.

That second part is the tell. Thread status filtering is not a feature you build for a demo. It is a feature you build when a customer has enough concurrent agent threads that they need to query them, not just create them. The moment you can filter threads by status, you have implicitly admitted that threads fail, stall, and complete, and that the caller needs to find the stalled ones without walking the whole list. That is an operational concern, not a prototyping one.

Workflows fit the same pattern. A workflow implies sequencing: step A, then step B, with state carried between them. Anthropic is not the first lab to reach this conclusion. OpenAI’s Agents SDK, Google’s Agent Development Kit, and a long tail of frameworks like LangGraph and CrewAI all converged on the same shape, which is a graph of steps with handoffs. The interesting question is not whether Anthropic ships workflows. It is whether Anthropic ships them in a way that keeps developers inside the Anthropic API surface rather than pushing them to a third-party orchestrator.

## The analytics types are the quieter move

The Chat and Cowork unified analytics metrics are less obviously about agents and more about Anthropic’s product portfolio. Chat is the consumer and enterprise chat surface. Cowork is the team-facing product. “Unified analytics metrics” typed in the SDK means a developer can now pull usage and performance data for both through one shape, rather than two.

Why does that matter for an SDK release? Because it signals that Anthropic wants the same developer writing against the same client library whether they are building on the consumer chat product or the team product. That is a consolidation play. A unified metrics type is a small thing, but it is the kind of small thing that shows up right before a company starts telling developers “build once, deploy across our surfaces.”

Anthropic's Python SDK v1.12.0 Ships Haiku 5.5 and Typed Computer-Use Tools — Tessera

# Anthropic's Python SDK v1.12.0 Ships Haiku 5.5 and Typed Computer-Use Tools

Anthropic's anthropic-sdk-python v1.12.0 adds claude-haiku-5-5, typed computer and browser tool calls, and model lifecycle fields. The quiet release is the interesting one.

 Tessera Newsroom · 5 min read · October 9, 2026 

FIGURE T-2026-1282

The gist

- Anthropic's SDK v1.12.0 adds claude-haiku-5-5 alongside typed computer and browser toolset calls, suggesting Haiku as default agent driver.
- Typed toolsets move guardrails into the SDK, letting developers validate, log, retry, and refuse browser actions instead of parsing loose payloads.
- Bug fixes address lost-response memory edits and dropped empty strings in query params, revealing Managed Agents production failure modes.

Anthropic shipped anthropic-sdk-python v1.12.0 on October 7, and the top line of the changelog is a model most people have not heard of: `claude-haiku-5-5`. It arrives in the same release as typed computer and browser toolset tool calls, a `disabled` flag on thinking types in model capabilities, and web search plus code execution support declared at the capability layer. None of that is a launch event. All of it is a tell about how Anthropic expects developers to wire agents together over the next two quarters.

The version bump is minor, 1.11.0 to 1.12.0, and there is no blog post, no keynote, no pricing page update attached. The release landed at 17:57 UTC from the `stainless-app` account, the bot that publishes SDKs generated by Stainless from Anthropic’s OpenAPI spec. That detail matters more than it looks. Anthropic’s SDKs are largely machine-generated from the API schema, which means the changelog is close to a raw diff of the API surface itself. When the SDK adds a model ID and a toolset type, the API gained them first.

## Haiku 5.5 exists now

The commit `f6346e6` adds `claude-haiku-5-5` alongside the typed tool calls. Anthropic has not published a model card, context window, or pricing for it in this release. What the SDK tells us is narrower and still useful: the model is addressable from the Python client, and it is grouped in the same commit as computer-use and browser tooling.

That grouping is the story. Haiku has historically been the cheap, fast tier, the one you reach for when Sonnet or Opus is overkill. Pairing a new Haiku with typed computer and browser toolsets suggests Anthropic wants the low-cost tier to be the default driver for agent loops that click, type, scroll, and fetch. A computer-use agent that runs on Opus pricing is a demo. One that runs on Haiku pricing is a product.

## Typed tools are the real change

“Typed computer and browser toolset tool calls” is dense, but it describes a concrete shift. Earlier computer-use integrations handed the model screenshots and coordinate actions as loosely structured payloads. Typed tool calls mean the client library now exposes those actions as named, schema-checked types. For a Python developer, that is the difference between parsing a dictionary and getting autocomplete on a `ToolUseBlock` with a known shape.

Typed toolsets are how you get agents that survive contact with production. If a browser action is a typed call, you can validate it, log it, retry it, and refuse it. If it is a blob, you write defensive code forever. Anthropic is moving the guardrails from the developer’s application into the SDK, which is the same play every serious agent platform is running right now.

The release also adds `url_sources` to the Managed Agents `web_fetch` tool config, and declares web search and code execution as model capabilities. Read together: the SDK is starting to describe what a model can do, not just how to call it. `web_fetch` with explicit URL sources is a constrained fetch, the kind you want when an agent should read a specific page rather than roam.
